title: How high is London's winter Sun?
hook: In December, how high does the noon Sun climb above London's horizon?

knows: that the Sun is lower in winter
that the Earth's axis is tilted
doesNotKnow: how low the winter noon Sun is at a mid-latitude city
that noon height is 90° minus latitude, plus or minus the tilt

misconception: The winter Sun in a mid-latitude city is only a little lower than at the equinox.
objective: The learner can explain that the noon Sun's height is 90° minus latitude plus the Sun's declination, so in London it is about 62° in June, 38° at the equinox and 15° in December: 47° apart, twice the tilt.

claims.text: In London the Sun is about 15° above the horizon at noon on 21 December, 38.5° at the equinox and 61.9° on 21 June.
claims.source: Noon altitude = 90° - latitude + declination (any astronomy text, e.g. Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms, ch. 13; from memory). Latitude 51.5072°N; declination ±23.44° at the solstices. 15.05°, 38.49°, 61.93° (noonAltitude in Demo.tsx). Geometric: no refraction (adds about 0.1° at 15°; brief). Uses the solstice declination, not the exact value on 21 December of a given year. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node: 90 - 51.5072 + dec = 15.05, 38.49, 61.93 deg for dec = -23.44, 0, +23.44; matches the stage (15.1/38.5/61.9 to 1 d.p.). Noon altitude = 90 - |lat - dec| for an observer north of the tropics is the standard formula.

51.5072°N, 0.1276°W (gazetteer coordinates for central London; from memory, not checked online). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): London 51.5072N, 0.1276W (standard gazetteer value for central London, matches Wikipedia infobox).

claims.text: The Earth's axis is tilted about 23.44°, so the noon Sun swings 23.44° above and below its equinox height.
claims.source: Obliquity of the ecliptic 23.44° (Astronomical Almanac; from memory, not checked online). Changes by about 0.013° per century. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Mean obliquity 23.44 deg (J2000 23.4393; 23.436 now), decreasing about 0.013 deg per century (46.8 arcsec/century).

claims.text: London's winter noon Sun is about 46.9° lower than its summer noon Sun, twice the tilt.
A sunbeam arriving at height h above the horizon covers 1/sin(h) times the ground it covers when the Sun is overhead: about 3.9 times at 15.1° and 1.1 times at 61.9°.
claims.source: Light per unit of level ground scales with sin(altitude): sin 15° / sin 62° = 0.29. Path length through the atmosphere is about 1/sin(altitude) for altitudes above about 10° (plane-parallel air mass), about 3.9 at 15°. Stated qualitatively in the reveal; numbers not shown. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node: sin 15 / sin 61.93 = 0.29 (ground light per area scales with sin altitude); plane-parallel air mass 1/sin 15 = 3.9 (Kasten-Young about 3.8), so 'more air' holds. | v2 (2026-10-14): claim text rewritten to match the revised stage; previous verification void, needs re-check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 17): Node: Dec altitude 90 - 51.5072 - 23.44 = 15.0528 deg; 1/sin = 3.850, which the reveal and readout print with f1 as '3.9', not '3.8'. June 61.9328 deg: 1/sin = 1.133, '1.1' (right). Fix (builder): claim text 'about 3.9 times at 15.1 deg'. | v3 (2026-10-14): text/stage revised after fact-check pass; previous verification void, needs re-check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 19): Node: Dec 90 - 51.5072 - 23.44 = 15.0528 deg (f1 '15.1'), 1/sin = 3.850 -> f1 '3.9'; June 61.9328 deg ('61.9'), 1/sin = 1.133 -> '1.1'. Geometry: a beam of cross-section A lands on A/sin(h) of level ground. The reveal prints these same f1 values.

claims.text: For places north of the tropics (24°N and up), the Sun's height at noon is 90° minus your latitude plus the Sun's tilt offset for the date (+23.44° in June, 0° at the equinox, −23.44° in December).
claims.source: Standard solar-noon altitude formula 90 - latitude + declination (e.g. Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms, ch. 13 / any positional-astronomy text); the stage computes it with altAt() and the lat slider shows it for other latitudes (0 to 60 N). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 17): 90 - lat + dec is the noon altitude only where the Sun culminates south of the zenith (lat >= dec). The stage's latitude slider runs 0 to 60N, so on 21 June at 0-23N the readout prints e.g. '90 - 0.0 + 23.4 = 113.4' as the Sun's height, which is impossible (max 90; true value 66.6 deg to the north). Fix (builder): set the latitude slider min to 24N (or show 180 - x 'to the north' when x > 90), and qualify the claim 'for places north of the tropics'. | v3 (2026-10-14): text/stage revised after fact-check pass; previous verification void, needs re-check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 19): Re-check of the pass 17 dispute: Demo.tsx now has MIN_LAT = 24, MAX_LAT = 60. At 24N in June the formula gives 89.44 deg (< 90, Sun south of zenith); at 60N in December 6.56 deg (> 0). For lat >= dec the noon altitude is 90 - lat + dec (derivation from the meridian: zenith distance = lat - dec). Claim text now qualified 'north of the tropics'.

claims.text: An equinox is a spring or autumn day when day and night are nearly equal in length.
claims.source: Standard definition (e.g. US Naval Observatory, 'Equinoxes and Solstices'); the stage ignores atmospheric refraction. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 17): On an equinox day and night are only nearly equal: day exceeds night by several minutes because of refraction and the Sun's disc (USNO 'Equinoxes and Solstices' FAQ; timeanddate 'Equinox: almost equal day and night'). The company's own equinox-twelve-everywhere c5 (verified) says so. The stage note repeats 'day and night equal'. Fix (builder, claim and Demo.tsx note): 'a spring or autumn day when day and night are nearly equal'. | v3 (2026-10-14): text/stage revised after fact-check pass; previous verification void, needs re-check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 19): Re-check of the pass 17 dispute: claim and stage note (Demo.tsx line 140) now say 'nearly equal'. Matches USNO 'Equinoxes and Solstices' (day slightly longer than night because of refraction and the Sun's disc) and the company's verified equinox-twelve-everywhere c5.

recall.question: A city is at 40°N. Roughly how high is the noon Sun there at the December solstice?
